title: Swallowed something poisonous — do not make them sick
applies_to: Anyone who has swallowed, breathed in, or spilled on themselves something that is not food.

citations.source: WHO and IFRC International First Aid, Resuscitation and Education Guidelines 2020
WHO Guidelines for Establishing a Poison Centre
European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2021: Special Circumstances
citations.section: Poisoning: rescuer safety and initial care

steps.text: Find out what they swallowed, how much, and how long ago. Keep the container, and keep whatever is left.
Call for an ambulance, or call the poison line if your area has one. Read the name off the container to them, word for word.
Check whether they are awake and whether the chest is rising and falling normally.
Wipe out the mouth with a wet cloth, or let them rinse and spit. Do not let them swallow the rinse.
Do exactly what the ambulance or the poison line tells you about giving water. The right answer is different for a cleaner, for fuel, and for something from a packet.
If they stop answering you but are breathing normally, roll them onto their side with the head tipped a little down.
If it went on the skin or in an eye, take off the wet clothing and rinse with plenty of clean running water for 20 minutes.
Stay with them and keep watching the breathing. Poisons often take an hour or more to show what they do.
Take the container, or a photo of the label, with you to the hospital. It tells the doctors what to give.

do_not: Do not make them sick, by any means at all. Bringing it back up burns the throat a second time.
Do not give them salt water, milk, or anything to drink unless you have been told to.
Do not put your fingers in their mouth.
Do not breathe in the fumes yourself. Open the windows, or take them into fresh air.
Do not wait to see whether anything happens. Make the call while they still look well.
escalate_if: They stop breathing normally, or their lips turn blue — start pushing on the chest and keep the phone on.
They start shaking or jerking — protect the head and let it run its course.
Their mouth or throat is burned, or they are drooling and cannot swallow — that is a straight-to-hospital sign.
They are sweating heavily, drooling, and the black centres of the eyes have gone very small — say the word pesticide on the phone.
It was a child, and you cannot be sure how much is gone — always assume the whole container.
